items.title: Over a Bezout domain any unimodular row of length n is the first row of an invertible matrix
items.author: The Stacks Project Authors
items.work: Stacks Project, chapter more-algebra.tex (More on Algebra)
items.source_version: Stacks Project source tree, file more-algebra.tex, corpus local snapshot 20261012
items.difficulty_reason: The lemma takes a Bezout domain R, an integer n >= 1, and elements f_1, ..., f_n generating the unit ideal, and asserts the existence of an invertible n x n matrix over R whose first row is f_1 ... f_n (source lines 37925-37930). The proof notes that this follows from the earlier splitting lemma but supplies a direct inductive construction. For n = 1 the result holds. For n > 1, after renumbering so that f_1 is nonzero, the proof uses the Bezout hypothesis to choose f with (f) = (f_1, ..., f_{n-1}), takes an (n-1) x (n-1) matrix A whose first row is f_1/f, ..., f_{n-1}/f — which exists by the induction hypothesis, since those quotients generate the unit ideal — and chooses a, b with af - b f_n = 1, possible because 1 lies in (f, f_n) (proof lines 37933-37941). The explicit answer is then the product of the two displayed matrices, the left one having determinant 1 and hence being invertible, whose product therefore has the required first row and is invertible (proof lines 37942-37962). The non-routine content is the reduction of length n to length n - 1 by factoring out the generator of the ideal spanned by the first n - 1 entries, together with the determinant-one matrix that supplies the last column.
